mainTopic: עיר הנדחת: who counts as part of the city, how it is judged, and which property is destroyed
overview: The amud opens by closing an earlier discussion with קשיא. It then asks whether a city that turned to עבודה זרה on its own, with no outside instigators, becomes an עיר הנדחת; a proof from the משנה's women-and-children case is pushed away. Next the גמרא asks how a court finds out that most of the city strayed: רב יהודה says judge and imprison, עולא and רבי יוחנן say judge and stone one by one, and ריש לקיש says add courts, with the בית דין הגדול giving the final verdict. A ברייתא teaches that travelers become part of the city after thirty days, and רבא explains that this makes them residents, while twelve months makes them full citizens. The גמרא then works out which property is destroyed: righteous people's property inside the city, wicked people's property even outside it if it can be gathered in, but not הקדש. רב חסדא adds rulings on deposits and on half-owned animals and dough. Two questions end in תיקו: whether שחיטה helps the city's animal, and whether a righteous woman's wig is destroyed. Finally, רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא argue whether a city with no town square can become an עיר הנדחת.

steps.title: The Previous Challenge Remains Unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the earlier discussion by saying the challenge there was never resolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the previous discussion with one word: the challenge raised there has no answer. This closes that topic so a new one can begin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the גמרא says just קשיא, the objection stands. The opinion it was aimed at, here ריש לקיש's, is left with an unanswered problem. It is not formally thrown out, but nothing defends it.

keyTerms.meaning: A difficulty. The challenge stands without an answer.

steps.confusionAlert: This קשיא is not the start of a new challenge. It is the closing word of the discussion that came before this section.

phrases.english: It is a difficulty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the previous sugya, which comes before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The challenge against ריש לקיש from the previous discussion is left unresolved.

steps.title: What If the City Led Itself Astray?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a city counts as an עיר הנדחת if nobody from outside pushed them, and they turned to עבודה זרה on their own.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the people of the city went astray on their own, what is the law? The תורה says 'and they led astray,' which might mean only when others led them, not when they led themselves. Or maybe it counts even if they led themselves astray?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. Does the law of עיר הנדחת apply only when outside people led the city astray, or also when the people turned to עבודה זרה by themselves?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes people who 'went out and led astray' the city. One reading is that the law requires outside instigators. The other reading is that the instigators are just the usual case, and a city that strays on its own is just as guilty.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the scholars.
They were led astray by themselves, with no outside instigator.
And they led astray (the פסוק's word).
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה.

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
If they were led astray by themselves, what is the law?
The Merciful One said "and they led astray,"
phrases.notes: דברים 13:14

phrases.english: and not when they were led astray by themselves?
Or perhaps, even if they were led astray by themselves?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic after the previous discussion closed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a city that turned to עבודה זרה with no outside instigators become an עיר הנדחת?

steps.title: Attempted Proof from Women and Children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer from the משנה's rule that a city led astray by women and children is not an עיר הנדחת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if women and children led the city astray, the people are judged as individuals. Why? Let it be like they led themselves astray! This suggests a self-led city does not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from the משנה. Women and children have no real standing as instigators, so a city they led astray is almost like one that led itself, and the משנה says such a city is not an עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning runs like this. Women and children do not count as instigators, so their case is really a city that strayed on its own. The משנה says that city is not an עיר הנדחת, so maybe no self-led city is one.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, which introduces a proof.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If women and children led it astray,
phrases.notes: This is quoted from our משנה, which says such a city is not treated as an עיר הנדחת.

phrases.english: Why? Let it be like they were led astray by themselves!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question from step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That a city that led itself astray is not an עיר הנדחת.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: a city led astray by women and children is judged as individuals.

steps.title: Following Yourself Is Different from Following Women and Children
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. People who stray on their own are fully committed, but people who follow women and children are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: These people, who strayed on their own, are drawn after their own minds. Those people are drawn after women and children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 3. The two cases are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A city that turns to עבודה זרה by itself acts from its own full conviction, so it may well be an עיר הנדחת. A city that follows women and children is drawn along weakly and is not truly committed. The משנה's ruling therefore teaches nothing about the self-led case, and the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: After their own selves, meaning their own will.

steps.whatToRemember: The question of a city that led itself astray is left open. The women-and-children case does not prove it, because following your own mind is stronger than following weak leaders.

phrases.english: Those are drawn after their own selves,
phrases.notes: "Those" means a city that strayed on its own.

phrases.english: these are drawn after women and children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof; it does not decide the question from step 2.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The two cases differ: being led by your own will shows full commitment, while being led by women and children shows weak commitment.

steps.title: How Do We Determine That Most of the City Strayed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's requirement that most of the city be led astray and asks how the court actually carries this out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: until most of it is led astray. How do we do this in practice?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new line in the משנה, that a city counts only when most of it strayed. It asks for the practical procedure, which sets up the opinions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person needs a separate trial with witnesses, so the court cannot judge everyone at once. The problem is what to do with each guilty person until the court knows whether a majority has been reached. The punishment depends on that number, since individuals get stoning and a city's people get the sword.

keyTerms.meaning: Until most of it is led astray.
How do we act, meaning what is the procedure?

phrases.english: Until most of it is led astray.
How do we act?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the court do with each convicted person while it works out whether most of the city went astray?

steps.title: רב יהודה: Judge and Imprison
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the court judges each person and holds the guilty in prison until it knows whether a majority strayed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: they judge and imprison, judge and imprison.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question from step 5. Each guilty person is jailed until the count is done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding everyone lets the court wait until all the trials are finished. Then it knows whether the city is an עיר הנדחת, which means the sword, or just individuals, which means stoning. This way nobody is executed with the wrong punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: They imprison, holding someone in jail.
An אמורא who gives the first answer.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
They judge and imprison, judge and imprison.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Judge each person and imprison the guilty until the majority is determined.

steps.title: עולא: Imprisoning Delays Their Judgment
steps.stepSummary: עולא objects that holding sentenced people in prison delays carrying out their judgment, which is not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said to him: then you are delaying the judgment of these people!
steps.whatsHappening: עולא challenges רב יהודה's method from step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a person is convicted, his sentence should be carried out without delay. Under רב יהודה's method, the first people convicted would sit in prison, possibly for a long time, while the rest are tried. עולא sees that waiting as wrongly delaying their judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who disagrees with רב יהודה.

phrases.english: Ulla said to him:
It turns out that you are delaying
the judgment of these!
phrases.notes: "These" means the people already found guilty who are waiting in jail.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יהודה's answer in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's method of judging and imprisoning.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Holding convicted people while others are tried delays their judgment, which is not allowed.

steps.title: עולא: Judge and Stone
steps.stepSummary: עולא gives his own method: judge each person and stone the guilty right away, one after another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, עולא said: they judge and stone, judge and stone.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected רב יהודה's method, עולא offers his own answer to the question of step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person is executed right after conviction, so no judgment is delayed. Until a majority is reached, the guilty are treated as individuals, and individual idol worshippers are stoned. The text here only says they judge and stone, one after another.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, which introduces a replacement view.
They stone, the punishment of סקילה.

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה says to judge and imprison until the majority is known. עולא says this delays judgment, so the court should judge and stone each guilty person right away.

phrases.english: Rather, Ulla said:
They judge and stone, judge and stone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב יהודה's answer after the objection in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Judge each person and stone the guilty immediately, one after another.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש on judging a whole city
steps.stepSummary: An אמוראים dispute: רבי יוחנן says the court judges and stones each person in turn, and ריש לקיש says the number of courts is increased.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רבי יוחנן says the court judges one person and stones him, then judges the next and stones him. ריש לקיש says we set up more courts for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second dispute about the same question: how to judge a whole city without leaving guilty people waiting in prison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's method matches עולא's: judge and stone right away, one after another. ריש לקיש takes another approach. He sets up many courts so that everyone is judged at the same time, and then nobody has to wait.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)

phrases.english: It was stated:
Rabbi Yochanan says:
They judge and stone, judge and stone,
And Reish Lakish says:
We increase the courts for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel dispute about the same procedure question that רב יהודה and עולא discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: judge and stone one by one. ריש לקיש: add more courts so everyone is judged together.

steps.title: A whole city cannot be judged in local courts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this using רבי אושעיא's teaching that local courts judge individuals but not an entire city.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי חמא בר יוסי said in the name of רבי אושעיא that the פסוק says, "You shall take out that man or that woman." So a man or a woman is taken to your local gates for judgment, but a whole city is not taken to your gates.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea that ordinary local courts can judge the people of an עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Your gates" means the local court. The פסוק limits that court to judging individuals. A whole city must go before the בית דין הגדול, so adding local courts cannot simply solve the problem.

keyTerms.meaning: To your gates, meaning the local court

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rabbi Chama bar Yosei say
that Rabbi Oshaya said:
"And you shall take out that man
or that woman" —
phrases.notes: דברים 17:5

phrases.english: A man and a woman you take out to your gates,
phrases.notes: "Your gates" means the court in your own town.

phrases.english: but you do not take out
the entire city to your gates!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר יוֹסֵי אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the procedures in step 9, especially ריש לקיש's local courts.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that ordinary courts can judge the people of an עיר הנדחת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק limits local courts to judging individuals. Judging a whole city belongs only to the בית דין הגדול.

steps.title: Many courts investigate, the great court rules
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: many courts look into the cases, and then the people are brought to the בית דין הגדול, which gives the verdict and carries it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, more courts are set up and they examine the cases. Then the people are brought up to the בית דין הגדול, which finishes their verdict and executes them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adjusts ריש לקיש's method so that it fits רבי אושעיא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The work is split into two parts. The extra courts only investigate. The final sentence and the execution come from the בית דין הגדול. This way there is no delay, and the whole city is still judged by the right court.

phrases.english: Rather,
we increase the courts for them
and they look into their cases,
and we bring them up to the Great Court,
and they finish their verdict,
and they execute them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, מַרְבִּין לָהֶן בָּתֵּי דִינִין וּמְעַיְּינִין בְּדִינֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 10 by refining ריש לקיש's procedure.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the process: investigation in many courts, final ruling in the בית דין הגדול.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think the extra courts both judge and execute.
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra courts only examine the cases. The בית דין הגדול gives the verdict and carries it out.
steps.whatToRemember: For an עיר הנדחת, many courts examine the cases, but only the בית דין הגדול gives the final sentence.

steps.title: Travelers who stayed in the city
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a caravan that stayed thirty days and was led astray is treated like the townspeople (sword, property destroyed). If it stayed less time, its people are stoned as individuals and their property is saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says, "You shall surely strike the inhabitants of the city." The רבנן taught: A donkey caravan or camel caravan traveling from place to place stopped overnight in the city and was led astray along with it. If they had stayed there thirty days, they die by the sword and their property is destroyed. If less than that, they are stoned and their property is saved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next words of the משנה and asks who counts as an "inhabitant" of the city. A ברייתא answers using a caravan of travelers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thirty days makes the travelers part of the city's people, so they share the city's punishment of sword and loss of property. With fewer days they are treated as individual idol worshippers. They are stoned, but their property is not destroyed.

phrases.english: "You shall surely strike the inhabitants of the city, etc."
phrases.notes: דברים 13:16

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
The donkey caravan and the camel caravan
that travels from place to place,
that stayed overnight in it and were led astray with it —
if they stayed there thirty days,
they are put to death by the sword and their property is destroyed.
Less than this,
they are put to death by stoning and their property is saved.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הַכֵּה תַכֶּה אֶת יֹשְׁבֵי הָעִיר וְכוּ׳״. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on the next phrase of the פסוק and משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Thirty days of staying makes travelers count as inhabitants of the עיר הנדחת. With less time they are stoned as individuals and keep their property.
steps.confusionAlert: Strangely, the travelers who stayed longer get the sword, which is a lighter death than stoning, but they lose their property. That is the עיר הנדחת package: sword plus destroyed property.

steps.title: Another source says twelve months
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a contradiction: another ברייתא says a person needs twelve months in a city to be like its people.
steps.simpleTranslation: A contradiction was raised: How long must someone be in a city to be like the people of the city? Twelve months!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets two ברייתות against each other: one says thirty days, the other says twelve months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources seem to answer the same question: when does an outsider count as part of a town? Since they give very different amounts of time, they seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the people of the city

phrases.english: And a contradiction was raised:
How long must one be in the city
and be like the people of the city?
Twelve months!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּרְמִינְהִי: כַּמָּה יִהְיֶה בָּעִיר וְיִהְיֶה כְּאַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the thirty-day measure from step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The thirty-day rule in the caravan ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא requires twelve months to be like the townspeople, so thirty days seems too short.

steps.title: Citizen versus resident
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that twelve months makes someone a full citizen of the town, while thirty days makes him a resident.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is not difficult. This one, twelve months, is about becoming one of the town's citizens. That one, thirty days, is about becoming one of the town's residents.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא solves the contradiction by explaining that the two ברייתות describe two different levels of belonging to a town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Becoming a full member of the town takes twelve months. Simply counting as someone who lives there takes only thirty days. For עיר הנדחת, the פסוק says "inhabitants" (יושבי העיר), so being a resident is enough.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is not difficult:
this is for becoming one of the citizens of the town,
phrases.notes: "This" is the twelve-month source.

phrases.english: that is for becoming one of the residents of the town.
phrases.notes: "That" is the thirty-day source, which matches the פסוק's word "inhabitants" (יושבי).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא לְמִיהְוֵי מִבְּנֵי מָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two levels of status: full citizen versus resident.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think both sources measure the same status, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: Twelve months makes a citizen, and thirty days makes a resident. For עיר הנדחת, being a resident is enough.
steps.whatToRemember: Thirty days makes you a resident (יושב) of a town, and twelve months makes you a citizen (בן העיר). For עיר הנדחת, the resident level counts.

steps.title: A vow case supports the difference between a citizen and a resident
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא about vows shows the same split רבא made: twelve months makes someone one of the 'בני העיר', and thirty days makes him one of the 'יושבי העיר'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it is taught: if someone vowed not to benefit from the people of a city, he may not benefit from anyone who lived there twelve months, but he may benefit from someone who lived there less. If he vowed not to benefit from the residents of the city, he may not benefit from anyone who lived there thirty days, but he may benefit from someone who lived there less.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about vows to back up רבא's answer from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said twelve months makes you a full citizen and thirty days makes you a resident. This ברייתא uses exactly those two time periods for two different vow wordings, so it supports him. For עיר הנדחת the פסוק speaks of residents, so thirty days is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone bound by a vow not to get benefit from certain people
The people of the city, its full citizens (twelve months)
The residents of the city (thirty days)

steps.confusionAlert: Usually 'וְהָתַנְיָא' opens a challenge ('But it was taught...!'). Here it means 'And so it was taught.' It supports רבא and does not attack him.

phrases.english: And so it is taught: one who is forbidden by a vow to benefit from the people of the city,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ אָדָם שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּהָא שָׁם שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ –
phrases.english: if there is a person who stayed there twelve months,
it is forbidden to benefit from him;
less than that, it is permitted to benefit from him.

phrases.aramaic: בְּיוֹשְׁבֵי הָעִיר, אִם נִשְׁתַּהָא שְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם –
phrases.english: With the residents of the city: if he stayed thirty days,
phrases.notes: This means: if the vow was worded as 'the residents of the city.'

phrases.english: it is forbidden to benefit from him;
less than that, it is permitted to benefit from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's answer in step 14 with a matching ברייתא from the laws of vows.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's split: twelve months makes a citizen, thirty days makes a resident
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on vows that uses the same two time periods for 'בני העיר' and 'יושבי העיר'

steps.title: Which property of the city is destroyed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's פסוק, and a ברייתא learns from each part of it what is destroyed and what is spared.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Destroy it and all that is in it': this leaves out the righteous people's property outside the city. 'And all that is in it' includes the righteous people's property inside the city. 'Its spoils' means not the spoils that belong to Heaven. 'And all its spoils' includes the wicked people's property outside the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא that reads the פסוק word by word to decide which property gets destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are four rules. The righteous lose property inside the city but keep what is outside it. The wicked lose even what is outside it. Property belonging to Heaven (הקדש) is never destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: Property of the righteous people in the city
Property of the wicked people who worshipped idols
Spoils of Heaven, meaning property set aside for the מקדש (הקדש)

steps.whatToRemember: Righteous: inside is destroyed, outside is saved. Wicked: even outside is destroyed. הקדש is always saved.

phrases.aramaic: ״הַחֲרֵם אֹתָהּ וְאֶת כׇּל אֲשֶׁר בָּהּ״ כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: 'Destroy it and all that is in it,' etc.
phrases.notes: דברים 13:16. The גמרא is quoting the next line of the משנה.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
'Destroy it and all that is in it':
this excludes the property of the righteous that is outside it.
'And all that is in it':
this includes the property of the righteous that is inside it.
'Its spoils': and not the spoils of Heaven.
phrases.notes: דברים 13:17

phrases.english: 'And all its spoils':
this includes the property of the wicked that is outside it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַחֲרֵם אוֹתָהּ וְאֶת כׇּל אֲשֶׁר בָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The righteous lose property inside the city only. The wicked lose property outside it too. הקדש is spared.

steps.title: Why righteous people lose their property
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון explains that their money is what kept them living in a wicked city, so their money is lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: Why did the תורה say the righteous people's property inside the city should be destroyed? What made them live there? Their money. So their money is lost.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון gives the reason for the surprising rule from the last step that righteous people lose their property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems unfair that the righteous are punished. רבי שמעון answers that they stayed in that city because of their money. So the punishment hits the very thing that kept them there.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said:
For what reason did the Torah say
that the property of the righteous inside it shall be destroyed?
What caused them to live inside it?
Their money.
Therefore their money is lost.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind one of the rules in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Righteous people lose their property because their money is what kept them living in the city.

steps.title: Only property that can be gathered into the city
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא limits the rule about the wicked people's outside property: only property that can be brought into the city is destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'And all its spoils you shall gather' includes the wicked people's property outside the city. רב חסדא said: and only property that can be gathered into it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats one line of the ברייתא so that רב חסדא can add a limit to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'gather' the spoils into the square. So רב חסדא says the outside property of the wicked is destroyed only if it can be brought into the city. Property that cannot be gathered into the city is not included.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said; the גמרא is quoting an earlier teaching
Things that can be gathered into the city

steps.whyThisMatters: This limit is the background for the next problem with רב חסדא's ruling on deposits.

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from two steps back.

phrases.english: 'And all its spoils you shall gather':
this includes the property of the wicked that is outside it.
Rav Chisda said: and only with things that can be gathered into it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows one of the rules from step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wicked people's property outside the city is destroyed only if it can be gathered into the city.

steps.title: Deposits are permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that deposits (פקדונות) of the people of an עיר הנדחת are permitted and are not destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Deposits of the people of an עיר הנדחת are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a new ruling about deposits. The גמרא will now try to work out which case he means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His ruling sounds simple, but it is not clear whose deposits he means or where they are kept. The next steps test the possible cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Deposits, items left with someone to look after
A city whose people were led to worship idols

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: פִּקְדוֹנוֹת שֶׁל אַנְשֵׁי עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת מוּתָּרִין.
phrases.english: Deposits of the people of an idolatrous city are permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: פִּקְדוֹנוֹת שֶׁל אַנְשֵׁי עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת מוּתָּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from the same רב חסדא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Deposits connected to an עיר הנדחת are not destroyed.

steps.title: What case is he talking about? The first option is too obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רב חסדא means. If he means deposits of outsiders kept inside the city, that is obvious, because they are not the city's spoils.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is property of another city that is kept inside this one, it is obvious that it is permitted. It is not 'its spoils'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which case רב חסדא means and rules out the first option because it is too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק only destroys 'its spoils,' meaning property that belongs to the city's people. Outsiders' things kept there were never the city's property. So רב חסדא would have nothing new to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What is the case?

phrases.aramaic: אִי לֵימָא דְּעִיר אַחֶרֶת וְאִיתַנְהוּ בְּגַוַּהּ –
phrases.english: If we say they belong to another city and are inside it,
it is obvious that they are permitted,
it is not 'its spoils'!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי לֵימָא דְּעִיר אַחֶרֶת וְאִיתַנְהוּ בְּגַוַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts testing which case רב חסדא's ruling in step 19 could mean.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case רב חסדא means: whose deposits, and where they are kept.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Here the first option is ruled out because it would be obvious. Step 22 answers by going back to this option with a new detail: the resident accepted אחריות.

steps.title: The second option either contradicts him or repeats him
steps.stepSummary: If he means the city's own property kept in another city, there is a problem either way. If it can be gathered, why is it permitted? If it cannot be gathered, רב חסדא already said that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is their own property kept in another city. If it can be gathered into the city, why is it permitted? And if it cannot be gathered, he already said that once!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the other possible case and shows that it also fails, which puts רב חסדא's ruling in trouble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From step 18, the wicked people's outside property is destroyed if it can be gathered in. So if the deposit can be gathered in, permitting it goes against that rule. If it cannot be gathered in, it is already covered by his earlier rule, so this ruling would just repeat it.

keyTerms.meaning: Their own (belonging to the city's people)
But he already said it once!

phrases.english: Rather, it is their own and is in another city.
If it can be gathered into it, why is it permitted?
And if it cannot be gathered into it,
he already said it once!
phrases.notes: This points back to רב חסדא's rule in step 18: only property that can be gathered in is destroyed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ruling out the first case in step 20, the גמרא shows that the second case fails too.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's ruling that deposits are permitted (step 19)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma. If the deposit can be gathered in, permitting it goes against his rule in step 18. If it cannot be gathered in, the ruling only repeats that rule.

steps.title: The deposits are outsiders' property that a resident took responsibility for
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא is talking about outsiders' deposits inside the city, where the resident holding them accepted responsibility. You might think that makes them his own property, so he teaches that they are still permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. He really means property of another city deposited inside the condemned city. The case is where the resident accepted responsibility for it. You might have thought that once he accepted responsibility it counts as his own, so רב חסדא teaches us it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from steps 20-21 by explaining the exact case רב חסדא meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said outsiders' deposits are obviously permitted. The answer is that the case has a twist: the resident holding the deposit accepted אחריות, so he must pay if it is lost. That could make it look like his own property, so רב חסדא needed to teach that it is still not destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit, an item left with someone for safekeeping
Responsibility, a promise to pay if the item is lost or damaged
You might have said (introduces the mistaken thought)
It teaches us (that the mistaken thought is wrong)

steps.whatToRemember: Accepting responsibility for a deposit does not turn it into your own property. It still belongs to the outsider, so it is not destroyed with the עיר הנדחת.

phrases.english: No, really [it is property] of another city
that is deposited inside it.
phrases.notes: "Inside it" means inside the condemned city.

phrases.english: And here, what are we dealing with?
For example, where he accepted responsibility upon himself.
phrases.notes: "He" is the person in the condemned city who is holding the deposit.

phrases.english: You might have said:
since he accepted responsibility for it,
it is like his own?
So it teaches us [that it is not].

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם דְּעִיר אַחֶרֶת דְּמַפְקְדִי בְּתוֹכָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 by taking the first option from step 20 and adding a new detail to the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) with a מהו דתימא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the resident accepted אחריות, the deposit counts as his and should be destroyed.
steps.terutzMaskana: It still belongs to the outsider, so it is permitted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Outsiders' deposits held by a resident are permitted even if he accepted responsibility for them.

steps.title: Half-owned animal is forbidden, half-owned dough is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that an animal half-owned by the condemned city is fully forbidden, while dough half-owned by it is permitted for the outsider's half.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: An animal that is half the property of the condemned city and half the property of another city is forbidden. Dough that is half the property of the condemned city and half the property of another city is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a new ruling about items that are jointly owned by the condemned city and an outsider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases look the same, half and half, but they get opposite results. The animal is forbidden entirely, while the outsider's half of the dough is permitted. The reason is not stated yet, and the גמרא asks for it next.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said:
An animal, half of which belongs to the condemned city
and half to another city, is forbidden.
Dough, half of which belongs to the condemned city
and half to another city, is permitted.
phrases.notes: Only the outsider's half is permitted. The city's half is still destroyed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: בְּהֵמָה חֶצְיָהּ שֶׁל עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling by the same אמורא on a related topic: property that is partly the city's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A jointly owned animal is entirely forbidden. The outsider's half of jointly owned dough is permitted.

steps.title: Why the difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the animal and the dough are treated differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב חסדא's split ruling. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both items are half and half, so the different results need an explanation.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a shared animal is forbidden but shared dough is permitted.

steps.title: An animal cannot be divided, dough can
steps.stepSummary: An animal is treated as one undivided thing, so the forbidden half forbids all of it. Dough can be split, so each half keeps its own status.
steps.simpleTranslation: An animal is like something that is not divided. Dough is like something that is divided.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason for רב חסדא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A living animal cannot be cut in half while each owner keeps a usable share, so it stays one unit, and the forbidden half wins. Dough can easily be split into two separate pieces, so the outsider's half can be taken and kept.

keyTerms.meaning: It is like something that is not divided
It is like something that is divided

steps.whatToRemember: The rule depends on whether the item can be split. If it can be divided, the outsider's share is saved. If it cannot, the whole item is forbidden.

phrases.english: An animal is like something that is not divided,
dough is like something that is divided.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Whether the item can be divided determines whether the outsider's share is saved.

steps.title: Does slaughtering the city's animal save it from נבלה impurity?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא asks whether שחיטה of an animal of the עיר הנדחת at least keeps it from carrying the טומאה of נבלה. He gives two sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא asked: An animal of a condemned city, does שחיטה work on it to keep it pure from the impurity of נבלה? The תורה says "by the edge of the sword," so maybe it makes no difference whether it was slaughtered or killed in another way. Or perhaps, since he slaughtered it, the שחיטה does work?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא raises a question he cannot answer and lays out both sides of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the animal must be destroyed and may not be eaten. The only question is about טומאה. Side one: the פסוק "לפי חרב" treats every way of killing the same, so a slaughtered animal is no better than a נבלה. Side two: a proper שחיטה still has its normal effect of keeping the animal from being a נבלה.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (raises a question he does not know the answer to)
An animal that died without kosher slaughter, which carries טומאה
By the edge of the sword

steps.confusionAlert: This is not asking whether the animal may be eaten. It must be destroyed either way. The question is only whether it carries the טומאה of נבלה.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda asked:
An animal of a condemned city,
what is the law, is slaughter effective for it
to keep it pure from the impurity of a carcass?
The Merciful One said "by the edge of the sword,"
phrases.notes: דברים 13:16

phrases.english: so it makes no difference if he slaughtered it,
and no difference if he killed it in another way.
Or perhaps, since he slaughtered it,
the slaughter is effective for it?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב חִסְדָּא: בֶּהֱמַת עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question by רב חסדא about the city's animals.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether שחיטה prevents the טומאה of נבלה in an animal that must be destroyed.

steps.title: The question remains unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finds no answer, and רב חסדא's question stays open.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the law? Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רב חסדא's question without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides between the two sides, so the question is left as תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question is left unresolved

phrases.english: What [is the law]? Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the question of step 26 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether שחיטה saves the animal of an עיר הנדחת from נבלה impurity is undecided.

steps.title: What about the hair of righteous women?
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף asks whether the hair of righteous women in the condemned city must be destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף asked: The hair of righteous women, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף opens a new question about women's hair in the עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The property of righteous people in the city is destroyed, so רב יוסף asks whether their hair counts as such property. His question assumes that the hair of wicked women would surely be destroyed.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef asked:
The hair of righteous women, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב יוֹסֵף: שְׂעַר נָשִׁים צִדְקָנִיּוֹת מַהוּ?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question about what is included in the destruction.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the hair of righteous women must be destroyed.

steps.title: רבא questions the assumption behind the question
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: is the hair of wicked women even forbidden? He challenges the premise of רב יוסף's question.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Is that to say that the hair of wicked women is forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רב יוסף by questioning the assumption his question rests on. This sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף assumed that wicked women's hair is destroyed and asked only about righteous women. רבא's rhetorical question means that even wicked women's hair is not forbidden, so the question about righteous women falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introduces a challenge)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Is that to say that [the hair] of wicked women is forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to step 28 by attacking its starting assumption.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's assumption that wicked women's hair is destroyed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If even wicked women's hair is permitted, there is nothing to ask about righteous women.

steps.title: The פסוק includes only things ready to be gathered and burned
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק "gather and burn" includes only things that need nothing more than gathering and burning. Hair would first need to be cut off, so it is excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: "You shall gather and you shall burn." That means something missing only gathering and burning. It excludes this hair, which is missing cutting, gathering, and burning.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא proves from the פסוק that hair is not destroyed at all, whether the women are righteous or wicked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah describes destroying the spoils as gathering and burning. Hair attached to a person needs an extra step, cutting it off, before it can be gathered and burned. So it falls outside the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall gather and you shall burn

steps.whatToRemember: Only things that are ready to be gathered and burned are destroyed. Hair needs cutting first, so no woman's hair is destroyed.

phrases.english: "You shall gather and you shall burn" is written.
phrases.notes: דברים 13:17

phrases.english: Something that is missing nothing
except gathering and burning,
excluding this, which is missing
cutting off, gathering, and burning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבא's challenge in step 29.
steps.raayaObject: That no woman's hair is destroyed in the עיר הנדחת

steps.title: רבא reframes the question: a wig
steps.stepSummary: Since hair on the head was excluded, רבא says the real question was about a פאה נכרית (a wig).
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the question is about a wig.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rescues רב יוסף's question by moving it to a wig, since real hair was already ruled out. This sets up the next steps, where the גמרא defines the exact case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hair attached to the head can't be destroyed, because it would first need cutting (step 30). A wig is a separate object, so the question about a righteous woman's hair becomes a real question again.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; signals a new version that replaces the old one

phrases.english: Rather, Rava says:
[the question is] about a wig.
phrases.notes: Literally 'foreign hair,' meaning hair that didn't grow on her own head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves רב יוסף's question, now that real hair has been excluded, onto a wig.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a righteous woman's wig in the עיר הנדחת have to be destroyed?

steps.title: If the wig is on her head, it is like her body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If she is wearing the wig, it should count as part of her body and be spared.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the wig is attached to her body, it is like her body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the new question by asking what case it could mean. If the wig is on her head, the answer seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wig she is wearing counts as part of her body, just like her own hair. Then there would be nothing to ask, so the case must be something else.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If it is attached to her body,
it is like her body.
phrases.notes: And her body, like her own hair, is not destroyed, so there'd be no question.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's reframed question by asking which case it could mean.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A wig worn on the head is like the body, so the question would have an obvious answer.

steps.title: The case is a wig hanging on a peg
steps.stepSummary: The question is only needed when the wig is hanging on a peg, not on her head.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed only where the wig is hanging on a peg.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is a wig that is off her head, hanging on a peg. That makes it a real question again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the wig is off her head, it is no longer part of her body. Now we must decide which group of objects it belongs to.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (this specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is necessary only
where it is hanging on a peg.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 32 by limiting the case to a wig that is off her head.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wig is on her head, so it is obviously like her body.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wig is hanging on a peg, so its status is unclear.

steps.title: Is the wig like property or like clothing?
steps.stepSummary: Two sides: the hanging wig may be like the property of the righteous (destroyed), or like her clothing (spared), since she wears it in and out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it like the property of the righteous in the city, and so destroyed? Or perhaps, since she goes in and out wearing it, it is like her clothing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the two sides of רבא's question about the hanging wig.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: it is an object sitting in the city, like any belonging of the righteous, which is destroyed. Side two: she regularly wears it when she goes in and out, so it is like her clothes, which are not destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: She goes in and goes out

phrases.english: Like the property of the righteous inside it
is it considered, and so destroyed?
Or perhaps, since she goes in and out [wearing it],
it is like her clothing?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּנִכְסֵי צַדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּתוֹכָהּ דָּמֵי וְאָבַד? אוֹ דִלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the case is set, spells out the two possible answers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a wig hanging on a peg treated like the property of the righteous or like the woman's clothing?

steps.title: The wig question stays open
steps.stepSummary: תיקו: the question is left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot settle the wig question and leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides between 'property' and 'clothing,' so the question stays unresolved, just like רב חסדא's question in step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Hair on her head is not destroyed (it would need cutting). A wig on her head is like her body. A wig on a peg is an open question: property or clothing? תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand [unresolved].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the wig question without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The status of a righteous woman's wig hanging on a peg in the עיר הנדחת stays unresolved.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל: no square, no condemned city
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'gather its spoil into its square,' a ברייתא brings רבי ישמעאל: a city without a square cannot become an עיר הנדחת.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And all its spoil you shall gather into the midst of its square,' etc. The רבנן taught: if it has no square, it does not become an עיר הנדחת. These are the words of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the פסוק and brings a ברייתא. רבי ישמעאל says a city without a town square can never become an עיר הנדחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah requires the spoils to be gathered into the city's square. If that step is impossible, רבי ישמעאל holds the whole law of עיר הנדחת does not apply to that city.

keyTerms.meaning: The words of; this is the view of

phrases.english: "And all its spoil
you shall gather into the midst of its square," etc.
phrases.notes: דברים 13:17

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If it has no square,
it does not become a condemned city;
these are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין לָהּ רְחוֹב – אֵינָהּ נַעֲשֵׂית עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next phrase in the פסוק, about the city's square.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city with no square cannot become an עיר הנדחת.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: make a square
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא disagrees: if there is no square, one is made for the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: if it has no square, they make a square for it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives the opposite view: missing a square doesn't save the city, because we simply build one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, the square is only a step in carrying out the law, not a condition for it. So if it's missing, we create it and continue.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is not saying the city is spared. He is saying the opposite: it still becomes an עיר הנדחת, and we build a square for it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
If it has no square,
one makes a square for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: אֵין לָהּ רְחוֹב – עוֹשִׂין לָהּ רְחוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city with no square still becomes an עיר הנדחת, and a square is made for it.

steps.title: What is the root of their argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what underlying idea splits the two תנאים. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both of them read the same פסוק. The גמרא wants to find exactly which point of reading separates them.

phrases.english: With regard to what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the argument in steps 36 and 37.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What principle underlies the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא?

steps.title: Does 'its square' mean one from before, or one made now?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל reads ״רחובה״ as a square that existed from the start. רבי עקיבא reads it as including a square made now.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds 'its square' means one that existed from the start. The other Sage holds 'its square' can also mean one made now.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that they disagree about the meaning of the word ״רחובה״, 'its square.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל: 'its square' means the city's own square from before, so a newly built one doesn't count, and without a square the city can't be condemned. רבי עקיבא: a square built now is also 'its square,' so we build one and the law goes ahead.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל: no square means no עיר הנדחת, because ״רחובה״ means a square that was there from the start. רבי עקיבא: build a square, because ״רחובה״ also includes one made now.
steps.whyThisMatters: The whole argument comes down to how one word in the פסוק is read. This is a common pattern: a halachic argument based on a word's meaning.

phrases.english: One Sage holds: "its square"
phrases.notes: This is רבי ישמעאל.

phrases.english: means [one that existed] from the beginning;
and the other Sage holds: "its square"
phrases.notes: This is רבי עקיבא.

phrases.english: also means [one made] now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 38 by showing the argument is about how to read ״רחובה״.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree whether ״רחובה״ means only a square that existed from the start, or also a square made now.
